title: Ibn Sina and the Canon of Medicine
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, is one of the most important scientists of the Middle Ages. He was born in the year 980 in a village near Bukhara, which at the time was one of the greatest centres of learning in the world. His father was an official, and the family was wealthy enough to give the boy the best teachers. Ibn Sina was a prodigy: according to his own account, he had memorised the Quran by the age of ten, and he had become so skilled in medicine by the age of sixteen that established doctors came to him for advice. Today he is remembered above all as a physician and a philosopher.

When Ibn Sina was about seventeen, the ruler of Bukhara fell seriously ill, and the court physicians could not cure him. The young man was called, and he succeeded. As a reward, he was allowed to use the royal library, a collection so large that, in his words, he had never seen the like of it. He read hungrily, often through the night, and he later said that he had studied the books until he knew them thoroughly. This opportunity shaped his future, and it demonstrates the importance of libraries and of rulers who support learning.

Ibn Sina's life was not peaceful. When the Samanid dynasty fell and Bukhara was conquered, he left the city and spent the rest of his life moving from court to court in Persia, working as a physician and as an adviser to rulers. He wrote at astonishing speed, sometimes at night after a day of work, and in some periods he produced several pages every day. Illness and political trouble interrupted his career, and at one point he was imprisoned for several months. He died in 1037 in the city of Hamadan, at the age of about fifty-seven.

His most important work is the Canon of Medicine, completed around 1025. It is an enormous encyclopedia in five books, which gathered the medical knowledge of the Greeks, Persians, Indians and Arabs and added his own observations. The first book describes the principles of medicine and the causes of disease; the second lists hundreds of medicines made from plants, minerals and animal products; the third and fourth cover diseases of the body from head to foot; and the fifth contains recipes for compound drugs. The book was clear and well organised, and doctors found that they could use it as a reference for a particular problem.

Ibn Sina understood many things that were not widely accepted for centuries. He noticed that certain illnesses, such as tuberculosis, pass from one person to another, and he suggested that a sick person should be kept apart from the healthy. He described the importance of diet, exercise and sleep for health. He insisted that a new medicine should be tested before it was used, and he laid down rules for the testing: the drug must be free of other influences, it must be tried on a disease that is not complicated, and it must produce the same result every time. These rules anticipate the clinical trials of modern medicine.

The Canon of Medicine was translated into Latin in the twelfth century, and for about six hundred years it was the standard textbook in the medical schools of Europe, as well as in the Islamic world. Students in Italy, France and England studied his words, and his name remained on university reading lists long after his death. The book was printed in dozens of editions after the invention of printing. Ibn Sina also wrote The Book of Healing, a vast work of philosophy and science, which discussed logic, physics, mathematics and music as well as the soul.

Dr Zarina Mirzaeva, a historian of medicine in Tashkent, says that Ibn Sina's greatest lesson is that a scientist must observe carefully and think freely. In Bukhara, a statue and a museum honour his memory. The ordinary habits he recommended, such as moderate eating and regular exercise, are what doctors recommend today. Yet Dr Mirzaeva reminds students that Ibn Sina was also a hard worker, who sat for long hours with his books, and she says that genius without effort would never have produced the Canon. She hopes that young people will read his works, in translation if necessary, and learn from his curiosity.
